summary.text: A 59-year-old man was hospitalized with cough, phlegm and low-grade fever after strenuous exercise and exposure to rain, with brown sputum, fatigue, night sweats and poor eating. He had diabetes for over 20 years and hypertension for over 10 years, treated with metformin, acarbose and irbesartan. He was incorrectly diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia and given moxifloxacin and oseltamivir without obvious relief.

Examination found rales over the upper right lung. Chest CT showed a thick-walled cavity lesion about 9 cm across in the right upper lobe, read by the radiologist as probably neoplastic and by an AI system as a high-risk lung cancer nodule. Sputum and blood cultures had no positive results, mNGS of the lavage fluid was negative, and cytology showed no acid-fast or fungal organisms; the cytology micrograph led to a suspected diagnosis of acute fibrinous and organizing pneumonia.

After multidisciplinary discussion, the antibiotic was discontinued and methylprednisolone 40 mg was given intravenously each day. The cough disappeared six days later and reexamination CT showed a significant reduction of the lesion, and the caption states the cavity had disappeared. He went home on oral methylprednisolone 24 mg per day, reduced to 16 mg per day after a week.

At the 6-month checkup he had no symptoms and no apparent negative reactions to the steroids, and he was very satisfied with the treatment, which avoided invasive needle biopsies and surgical procedures.

article_limitations: Figure panels were pixel-inspected in the separate visual submission; the annotation figures keep caption-level status not_inspected.
The case text gives no calendar dates and almost no time anchors: the CT, laboratory tests and bronchoscopy are not placed relative to admission, so their times stay null.
AFOP is a suspected diagnosis from lavage-fluid cytology; the authors state there was no histologic diagnosis.
The captions print "mediation window", read in the visual submission as printed without correcting it.
Background and discussion statements about cavitary lung disease, tuberculosis, abscess, lung cancer and a previous AFOP case are not patient facts.
No supplements are listed in the source.
